# Collection Types
Collection types are used to store and process multiple values in a single variable. Python has four collection types, each of which is its own class:

  - [Lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_%28abstract_data_type%29) contain a flexible number of elements of any type.

  - [Tuples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuple) can contain elements of any type, just like lists, but they are immutable.

  - [Sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_%28abstract_data_type%29) are unordered collections that can contain each element only once.

  - [Associative arrays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associative_array) or dictionaries are mapping tables, i.e. they consist of key-value pairs.

This chapter first briefly introduces the four collection types. It then explains how to work with them, focusing in particular on lists.

## Lists
As with all types in Python, lists are created through assignment. When defining a list, the elements are enclosed in square brackets `[]` and separated by commas `,`. Lists can be concatenated with the `+` operator. `*` concatenates a list n times.

```{python}
text_variable = 'abc'

list1 = [1, 'xy', True, text_variable]
print(list1)

# Lists can also contain lists
list2 = [None, list1]
print(list2)

# Lists can be concatenated with + and *
print(list1 + list2)
print(list1 * 2)
```

An empty list can be created by assigning `[]`.

```{python}
empty_list = []
print(empty_list)
```

### Slicing: the access operator []
Access to individual or multiple elements of a list (and other collection types) is done via the access operator []. A section extracted from an object is called a slice, which is why the operator is also known as the slice operator.

#### Accessing individual elements
Elements are accessed via their index, starting at 0.

```{python}
print(list1)
print(list1[0])
print(list1[3])
```

Nested lists can be accessed with two consecutive access operators. The list `list2` contains a list with 4 elements at index position 1.

```{python}
print(list2)
print(list2[1])
print(list2[1][0], list2[1][1], list2[1][2], list2[1][3])
```

Negative indices can be used to access elements from the end. For example, -1 corresponds to the last element.

```{python}
print(list1)
print(list1[-1], list1[-3])
```

#### Accessing multiple elements
Index ranges can be addressed in the form `[start:stop:step]`. `start` is the first element addressed, `stop` is *the first element no longer addressed*, and `step` is the step size.

::: {.border}

| Access operator | Selection |
|---|---|
| list[start:stop] | Elements from start to stop - 1 |
| list[:] | All elements of the list |
| list[start:] | Elements from start to the end of the list |
| list[:stop] | Elements from the beginning of the list to stop - 1 |
| list[::3] | Selection of every third element |

&nbsp;

Negative values for `start`, `stop`, or `step` result in a backward selection of elements.

| Access operator | Selection |
|---|---|
| list[-1] | the last element of the list |
| list[-2:] | the last two elements of the list |
| list[:-2] | all elements except the last two |
| list[::-1] | all elements in reverse order |
| list[1::-1] | the first two elements in reverse order |
| list[:-3:-1] | the last two elements in reverse order |
| list[-3::-1] | all elements except the last two, in reverse order |

&nbsp;

(Examples by Greg Hewgill, available under the [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en) license on [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/a/509295). 2009)
:::

#### Strings
Sections can also be selected from strings using the slice operator.

```{python}
print('I am a string'[::2])
print('Hello World'[0:6])
print('abc'[::-1])
```

### List methods
Various methods are defined for the list type.

#### Determining elements

- `list.index(x, start, stop)` returns the index position of the first element x. The optional arguments `start` and `stop` allow you to restrict the search range.

- `list.count(x)` returns the number of times x occurs in the list.

- `list.reverse()` reverses the order of the list elements (this modifies the list!).

- `list.sort(reverse = False)` sorts the list; with the optional argument reverse = True, it sorts in descending order (this modifies the list!). The data types within the list must be sortable (i.e. all elements must be either numeric or characters).

```{python}
print(list1)

list1.reverse()
print(list1)

# True is counted as 1
print("True is counted as 1:", list1.index(1), list1.count(1))
```

#### Inserting elements

- `list.append(x)` appends a single element to the end of the list.

- `list.extend(collection)` appends all elements from the given `collection` to the end of the list. The collection can be a list, a tuple, a set, or a dictionary.

- `list.insert(i, x)` inserts element x at position i.

```{python}
print(list1, "\n")

list1.append('Hello')
list1.extend(['Hello', 'World!'])
list1.insert(2, '12345')

print(list1)
```

#### Removing elements

- `list.remove(x)` removes *the first* occurrence of element x in the list and raises a ValueError if x is not contained in the list.

- `list.pop(i)` removes the element at index position i. If no index is given, the last element is removed. The `list.pop(i)` method returns the removed element.

- `list.clear()` removes all elements from a list.

```{python}
list1.remove('Hello')
print(list1)

list1.pop(2)
```

#### Copying lists and list elements
In Python, lists don't contain data directly; instead, they consist of pointers to the memory locations of the elements they contain. If a list is created by assigning it to another list, the elements of the list are not copied — instead, both lists then access the same memory location.

```{python}
# Copying by assignment
list1 = [1, 'xy', True, text_variable]
print("list1:", list1, "\n")
list2 = list1

## Changing an element in list2
list2[0] = 'ABC'
print("list1 has also changed because of the assignment to list2:", list1, "\n")

```

To copy a list and create a new object in memory, the `list.copy()` method can be used. Using the access operator `[:]` also creates a new list in memory.

```{python}
# Using the list.copy() method
list1 = [1, 'xy', True, text_variable]
list2 = list1.copy()

## Changing an element in list2
list2[0] = 'ABC'
print("list1 remains unchanged by the assignment to list2:", list1, "\n")

# Using the slice operator
list1 = [1, 'xy', True, text_variable]
list2 = list1[:]

## Changing an element in list2
list2[0] = 'ABC'
print("list1 remains unchanged by the assignment to list2:", list1)
```

Copying list elements is unproblematic in this regard.

```{python}
# Using the slice operator
list1 = [1, 'xy', True, text_variable]
list2 = list1[0:2]

# Changing an element in list2
list2[0] = 'ABC'
print("list1 remains unchanged by the assignment to list2:", list1)
```

To check whether two objects share the same area of memory, you can compare the object ID using the `id()` function, or use the `is` and `is not` operators, which internally call the `id()` function.

```{python}
list1 = [1, 'xy', True, text_variable]
list2 = list1

print("ID of list1:", id(list1))
print("ID of list2:", id(list2))
print("ID of list1 equal to ID of list2:", list1 is list2)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Identity vs. equality

The `is` operator checks the identity of two objects, which distinguishes it from the logical operator `==`, which checks for equality of values. Since list1 and list2 contain the same elements, both identity and equality hold here. The difference between identity and equality can be illustrated using a single value (a syntax warning is suppressed in the code example below).

```{python}
#| warning: false

# Equality
print(1 == 1.0)
print(list1 == list2, "\n")

# Identity
print(1 is 1.0)
print(list1 is list2)
```

:::

## Tuples
Tuples are very similar to lists, but tuples are immutable data objects. This means that the elements of an existing tuple can neither be changed nor removed. Nor can new elements be added to a tuple.

Tuples are created with round brackets `()`, and the elements are separated by a comma `,`. A tuple with a single value is created with a comma in the form `(value, )`. The elements of a tuple can be accessed with the slice operator `[start:stop:step]`. Tuples can be concatenated with the `+` and `*` operators.

```{python}
tuple1 = (2, 7.8, 'Fire', True, text_variable)
tuple2 = (1, )

print(tuple1)
print(tuple1[2:4])
print(tuple1[::2])
print(tuple1[-1])
print(tuple1[2:4] + tuple2)
print(3 * tuple2)
```

### Copying tuples
Tuples behave the opposite way to lists when it comes to copying. The `.copy()` method is not defined for tuples. However, copying with the access operator `[:]` does cause two tuples to access the same memory location. When a tuple is reassigned, Python — as with any object — creates a new object in memory.

```{python}
# Copying by assignment
tuple1 = (1, 2, 3)
tuple2 = tuple1

## Reassigning the values of tuple1
tuple1 = (4, 5, 6)
print(f"The values stored in tuple2 are unchanged:\n{tuple1} {tuple2}\n")

# Copying with the slice operator
tuple1 = (1, 2, 3)
tuple2 = tuple1[:]
print(tuple2 is tuple1)

## Reassigning the values of tuple1
tuple1 = (4, 5, 6)
print(tuple1, tuple2)
```

## Sets
In Python, sets can be created with the `set()` function, e.g. from a list or a tuple, or by using curly braces `{}` (an empty set can only be created with `set()`, since `{}` creates an empty dictionary). Sets are unordered collections, so the elements have no particular order.

```{python}
my_list = [1, 1, 5, 3, 3, 4, 2, 'a', 123, 1000, ('tuple', 5)]
print("The my_list object as a set:\n", set(my_list))

my_set = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 1000, ('tuple', 5), 'a', 123}
print("A set can also be created using curly braces:", my_set)
```

Sets can be used, for example, for comparison operations.

```{python}

set_a = set('Python')
set_b = set('is great')

# unique characters in a
print("Set a:", set_a)

# characters in a but not in b
print("Set a - b:", set_a - set_b)

# characters in a or b
print("Set a | b:", set_a | set_b)

# characters in a and b
print("Set a & b:", set_a & set_b)

# characters in a or b, but not in both (XOR)
print("Set a ^ b:", set_a ^ set_b)
```

### Copying sets
Sets behave like tuples, with the difference that the `.copy()` method is defined for sets. However, the access operator `[]` cannot be applied to sets.

```{python}
# Copying by assignment
set1 = {1, 2, 3}
set2 = set1
print(set1 is set2)

## Reassigning set1
set1 = {4, 5, 6}
print(f"The values stored in set2 are unchanged:\n{set1} {set2}")

# Copying using the .copy() method
set1 = {1, 2, 3}
set2 = set1.copy()
print(set1 is set2)

## Reassigning set1
set1 = {4, 5, 6}
print(f"The values stored in set2 are unchanged:\n{set1} {set2}")

```

## Dictionaries
Dictionaries consist of key-value pairs. The keys can be numbers or strings, and each key may occur only once. Dictionaries are defined with curly braces `{}`. The keys and their associated values are separated by a colon `:`. Values are accessed with the access operator `[]`, which contains the key or keys. Access via the index position of the keys is not possible, since numbers are interpreted as keys.

```{python}
dictionary1 = {1: 'abc', 'b': [1, 2, 3], 'c': ('tuple', 5, 6)}
print(dictionary1, "\n")

print("Values of key 1:", dictionary1[1])
print("Values of key 'b':",  dictionary1['b'])
```

The keys of a dictionary can be accessed with the `dictionary.keys()` method, and the values with the `dictionary.values()` method.

```{python}
print("Keys:", dictionary1.keys(), "\n")
print("Values:", dictionary1.values())
```

### Copying dictionaries
Dictionaries behave like lists when copied, meaning that copying by assignment causes dictionaries to share the same memory area.

```{python}
# Copying by assignment
print("dictionary:", dictionary1, "\n")
dictionary2 = dictionary1

## Changing an element in dictionary2
dictionary2[1] = 'ABC'
print("dictionary1 has also changed because of the assignment to dictionary2:\n",
       dictionary1, "\n")

# Using the dictionary.copy() method
dictionary1 = {1: 'abc', 'b': [1, 2, 3], 'c': ('tuple', 5, 6)}
dictionary2 = dictionary1.copy()

## Changing an element in dictionary2
dictionary2[1] = 'ABC'
print("dictionary1 remains unchanged by the assignment to dictionary2:\n",
       dictionary1, "\n")

```

## Overview of collection types
| Feature                                        | Lists | Tuples | Sets | Dictionary |
|------------------------------------------------|--------|-------|--------|------------|
| Description                            | flexible number of elements of any type | elements of any type, immutable | unordered collection, each element contained only once | mapping table of key-value pairs |
| Memory area shared on assignment          | yes     | yes (but immutable)  | yes (but access operator not applicable)   | yes         |
| .copy() method defined                      | yes     | no  | yes     | yes         |
| Slice operator applicable                       | yes     | yes    | no     | yes (by key) |

&nbsp;

## Deleting: the del keyword
The `del` keyword can be used to delete collection types, elements, or slices.

```{python}
# Deleting a list
del list1

# Deleting an index range from a list
print("List before deletion:", list2)
del list2[1:3]
print("List after deletion:", list2)

# Deleting a key from a dictionary
print("Dictionary before deletion", dictionary1)
del dictionary1[1]
print("Dictionary after deletion", dictionary1)
```

## Functions
The collection types can be converted into each other.

```{python}
dictionary = {1: 'Tomcat', 2: 'Ferry', 3: 'Doe'}
print( (my_list := list(dictionary)) )
print( (my_set := set(my_list)) )
print( (my_tuple := tuple(my_set)) )

```

Some useful functions can also be applied to collection types:

* `len()` returns the number of elements in a collection type.
* `min()`, `max()`, `sum()` return the minimum, maximum, or sum of a collection type, respectively (for dictionaries, these functions operate on the keys).

## Operations: using loops
A `for` loop is used to apply arithmetic and logical operators to the elements stored in a collection type. In the following example, a list `numbers` is iterated over, the numbers stored in it are squared, and each result is appended to the list `squared_numbers`. It is also checked whether the squared numbers are evenly divisible by 3, and the result of that check is stored in a list `modulo_3`.

::: {#lst-squared-numbers}
``` {python}
numbers = list(range(1, 11))

squared_numbers = [] # the list must be created before the loop
modulo_3 = [] # create an empty list before the loop

for number in numbers:
  squared_number = number ** 2
  squared_numbers.append(squared_number)
  modulo_3.append(squared_number % 3 == 0)

print(squared_numbers)
print(modulo_3)
```

:::

## Sample solution: exercises collection types

1. Squared numbers divisible by 3
``` {python}
numbers = list(range(1, 11))

squared_numbers = [] # the list must be created before the loop
modulo_3 = [] # create an empty list before the loop

for number in numbers:
  squared_number = number ** 2
  if squared_number % 3 == 0:
    squared_numbers.append(squared_number)

print(squared_numbers)
```

2. Converting speeds

```{python}
# Free-form input
## start = int(input("Enter the start value in kilometers per hour."))
## end = int(input("Enter the end value in kilometers per hour."))
## output_steps =  int(input("Enter the number of steps to output."))

# Fixed values for the solution
start = 5
end = 107
output_steps = 8

# Create the list of km values
step_size = (end - start) / (output_steps - 1)
km_list = []
for i in range(output_steps):
    km_list.append(round(start + i * step_size))

# Conversion
# meters = 1000 * kilometers
# seconds = hours * 60 * 60
m_list = []
for value in km_list:
    m_list.append(round((value * 1000) / (60 * 60), 2))

# Output
print(f"Step size: {step_size:.2f}")
print("Kilometers per hour")
print(km_list)
print("Meters per second")
print(m_list)
```

3. Sorting: bubble sort algorithm
```{python}

# static list, text output
my_list = list(range(9, 0, -1))

if len(my_list) > 1:

    print("List at the start\t\t  :", my_list)

    # outer loop
    step = 0
    for i in range(len(my_list) - 1):

    # inner loop
        for j in range(len(my_list) - 1):
            if my_list[j] > my_list[j + 1]:
                my_list[j], my_list[j + 1] = my_list[j + 1], my_list[j]

        step += 1
        print("List after step ", step, ":", my_list)

    print("\nSorted list:", *my_list) # * suppresses the commas between list elements

else:
    print("The list must contain at least two elements!")

```
